info.title: Erly adverse-search API
info.description:
Adverse-media screening. Free and open-source sources only.

Three things about this API are unusual, and all three are deliberate:

- **A result has three independent dimensions, not one status.** `execution`,
  `findings` and `coverage` answer different questions: whether the run finished,
  what was found, and whether everything promised was actually searched. A run that
  succeeded with no findings and a run whose sources were all blocked are not the
  same result, and no field collapses them.
- **An entitlement denial is not throttling and not a coverage gap.** It is a 403
  with a specific code, and it is never retryable.
- **Sparse identity input is accepted and stays unresolved.** A missing date of birth
  is never inferred, and a name is never split into given and family parts.

get.description: Version-neutral and unauthenticated: a load balancer cannot authenticate, and a version bump must not turn every probe into a 404 — which reads as "the service is down".
Whether this instance will accept traffic. It deliberately does not say why not.
Separate from the public probes because it discloses which dependency is degraded, which tells an attacker where to push. Requires `platform:read_health`.

Redirects to the identity provider with PKCE (`S256`); the verifier never leaves the service. Version-neutral, because the redirect URI is registered at the provider and must not change with an API version.

302.description: Redirect to the identity provider. Sets two short-lived handshake cookies.

get.summary: Complete sign-in and establish the session
get.description: Exchanges the authorisation code, then issues the HTTP-only session cookie and the readable CSRF cookie. A mismatched `state` is rejected.

302.description: Signed in; redirect to the panel.

post.summary: Revoke the session
post.description: POST rather than GET: a GET logout can be fired by any page that embeds an image.

get.description: What the panel needs to render its shell. Carries no token and no session identifier.

post.summary: Create a service-owned identity snapshot (FR-01)
post.description:
The full name is stored as written, in its original script, and is **never split**
into given and family parts. Splitting destroys patronymic chains, mononyms and
every naming system that puts the family name first — silently, at intake, before
any matching can compensate. Normalised comparison forms are derived alongside the
original, never in place of it.

Sparse input is accepted. A missing date of birth stays missing; the subject simply
remains unresolved rather than being completed by inference.

`externalSubjectRef` and `externalCaseRef` are recorded for correlation only. They
are neither a lookup instruction nor an authorisation credential.

get.summary: Read one pinned version of a subject
get.description: Versions are immutable. A data update creates a new one, and a historical search keeps the version it ran against, so a past result can still be explained.

post.summary: Accept a search for execution
post.description:
Returns **202 Accepted** with a status URL, not a result. Returning 200 with a
result-shaped body would invite a caller to read "accepted" as "completed, nothing
found".

Send `Idempotency-Key` to make submission safe to retry: an identical request
returns the original run with **200**, a changed body under the same key returns
**409**, and two concurrent identical submissions produce exactly one run.

The scope in the request is what is being *asked for*. What was actually searched
comes back as the coverage statement, and it may be narrower.

parameters.name: Idempotency-Key
parameters.description: Tenant-scoped. Without it there is no duplicate protection, and the caller owns the consequences.

200.description: Idempotent replay: this exact request was already accepted, and this is the original run.

get.summary: List searches for the caller's tenant
Read a search and its three result dimensions
get.description:
`execution`, `findings` and `coverage` are independent and must be read together.
`SUCCEEDED` with `NO_MATCHES_FOUND` and `INCOMPLETE` coverage means the run
finished, found nothing, **and did not search everything it promised** — which is
not a clean result, and must never be presented as one.

`progress` never carries a fabricated percentage: it reports stages completed and
the cascade rung reached, or nothing.

200.description: The search. The `ETag` header carries the current revision; quote it in `If-Match` on any action that changes the run.

ETag.description: The current revision, quoted. Send back as `If-Match`.

get.summary: Read what a search produced, and what it could not
get.description:
Returns the findings **together with the three result dimensions**. That pairing is
deliberate: a client that reads findings alone cannot tell a genuinely clean run
from one in which every source was blocked, because both return an empty array.

A `band` is never a score and never arrives alone — `axes` and `rationale` travel
with it, because FR-08 requires the four contributing values be retained verbatim
and FR-13 requires the reviewer be able to see why. There is no numeric risk score
anywhere in this response, by design (invariant I9).

`rejectedLeads` are candidates that were found and **not** promoted, each with its
reason. They are returned rather than discarded because a pipeline that silently
drops what it decided against cannot be audited (FR-06).

When there are no findings, `noMatchStatement` is present and names what was
searched, what was not, and what that does and does not mean. It never says
"clear", "clean" or "no adverse media".

`mode: "MOCK"` means every record came from fixture data and no live source was
contacted. It is never servable as a live result.

200.description: The findings, the rejected leads, and the coverage they sit inside.

get.summary: Read the frozen FR-02 association graph for a search
get.description:
The graph **as it was when the search ran**, not a fresh look at the register.
A registry correction next month must not rewrite what a historical search
explained, so a refresh produces a new snapshot linked to this one rather than
mutating it.

Three things here are routinely misread and are therefore separate fields.

A `coverage.outcome` of `UNKNOWN` means **no approved register covers the
jurisdiction, so none was asked**. It is not a worse `INCOMPLETE`, and neither
value ever means no associations exist.

`unresolvedCandidates` are people of the same name the graph could **not**
attribute to the subject. They are returned rather than hidden, so a reviewer can
see that the register held more than one such person. They are not findings.

`edges[].attachesCompany` is the only field that says whether an edge may anchor
a company query. An edge can be resolved and still out of scope, so it is stated
rather than left to each consumer to recompute differently.

post.summary: Cancel a search that is still running
post.description:
Requires `If-Match` carrying the revision the caller last read. Without it the
request is rejected: a cancellation issued against a run whose state has since
changed is a decision made on information that is no longer true.

A stale `If-Match` returns **409** with a `conflict` object carrying the current
revision and the current execution state, so the caller can see what changed and
re-submit deliberately rather than retrying blindly.

Cancellation is **final and does not rewrite history**. Stages that had already
succeeded stay succeeded, and a worker that completes after the cancellation has
its result discarded rather than applied — the run is not re-opened by work that
arrives late.

Cancelling an already-terminal run returns **409 `ALREADY_TERMINAL`**, not a
silent success. "Nothing to do" and "done" are different answers.

parameters.name: If-Match
parameters.description: The revision from the last read, as returned in `ETag`.

example.reason: Requested by the client; screening no longer required.

200.description: Cancelled. The run is terminal and its revision has advanced.

409.description: Either the revision was stale (`REVISION_CONFLICT`, with a `conflict` object naming the current revision and state) or the run is already terminal (`ALREADY_TERMINAL`).

post.summary: Propose a new version of a source, taxonomy or policy
post.description:
`collection` is one of `sources`, `taxonomy` or `policies`. All three share one
lifecycle: **PROPOSED -> AWAITING_APPROVAL -> APPROVED -> ACTIVATING -> ACTIVE**,
with `SUSPENDED`, `SUPERSEDED` and `RETIRED` alongside it.

A proposal is always the *next* version. A version past `PROPOSED` is immutable, so
changing an active source means proposing its successor - which is what lets a
historical search still explain itself under the version it actually ran on.

Taxonomy and policy versions are identified by the calling **tenant**; a source is
identified by its `recordId`, and source configuration is shared across tenants.

200.description: Versions, newest first within each record.

get.description: Returns the revision as an `ETag`. Every state-changing admin call requires it in `If-Match`, so an administrative decision cannot be taken on state the caller has not seen.

put.description: Permitted only while `PROPOSED`. Once submitted, content is frozen - otherwise the approver approves one thing and a different thing activates.

parameters.name: If-Match
parameters.description: The revision from the last read, as returned in `ETag`.

post.summary: Submit, approve, request changes, suspend, restore or retire
post.description:
**Four eyes.** `APPROVE`, `REQUEST_CHANGES` and `RESTORE` must be performed by a
different authorised user from the one who proposed the version (section 4.2, test
T45). The refusal is recorded in the audit trail, not only returned as a 403.

**Suspension is deliberately asymmetric.** `SUSPEND` needs no second person -
requiring one to *stop* using a source is how a harmful source stays live over a
weekend. `RESTORE` needs both a second person and a fresh rights clearance, and
lands in `ACTIVATING` rather than going straight back to `ACTIVE`.

A reason is required for every action except `SUBMIT`, and is recorded (SEC-06).

parameters.name: If-Match
parameters.description: The revision from the last read, as returned in `ETag`.

post.summary: Activate an approved version, through the SEC-05 rights gate
post.description:
Activation is two steps: `APPROVED -> ACTIVATING`, then the rights clearance, then
`ACTIVATING -> ACTIVE`. The clearance is stored on the version either way.

Returns **200 with the clearance whether or not it passed**, rather than a 403 on
refusal. A refusal is a result the administrator has to read - which operation,
which reason code, which policy - and an error body carrying one message would lose
exactly that. Read `activated` and the version `status` for what happened: `ACTIVE`,
or back to `APPROVED` with the clearance attached.

A `DENY` is never upgraded by an approval reference: a prohibited collection method
- a CAPTCHA, a login wall, a paywall - cannot be licensed by anyone.

parameters.name: If-Match
parameters.description: The revision from the last read, as returned in `ETag`.

200.description: The activation attempt and its clearance.

get.summary: What this service can and cannot do in a jurisdiction
get.description:
Every capability carries a status - `SUPPORTED`, `PARTIAL`, `UNKNOWN` or
`UNSUPPORTED` - and an `emptyResultMeans` field saying what an empty result from it
may be called. **Only `SUPPORTED` yields `NO_FINDINGS`**; everything else yields
`NOT_ESTABLISHED`, and must never be rendered as a clean result.

`UNKNOWN` and `UNSUPPORTED` are not the same. `UNSUPPORTED` is a finished
investigation - there is no way to do this here. `UNKNOWN` is an unfinished one.

Readable by anyone holding `coverage:read`, including an auditor. What the service
cannot do is not a secret; hiding it is how a reviewer comes to believe an empty
result was a search.

put.summary: Declare or revise a capability coverage status
put.description: A coverage status is an assertion about what this product can do in a country, and it reaches a reviewer unmediated - so it needs `source:approve`, not merely `source:propose`, and it records who declared it and what evidence it rests on.

200.description: The revised coverage statement for that jurisdiction.

get.summary: Breaker state, budget spend and kill switch, per source
get.description:
Source health is a **separate mutable document** from the approved source version,
and the separation is visible here: this response carries no approved field, and
`SourceContent` carries no observation. The approved version says what is
*permitted*; health says what is *happening*.

Needs `platform:read_health`, which `platform_operator` holds and which grants no
access to a single customer finding. Breaker state and budget spend are properties
of the publisher, not of anybody customer data - an operator must be able to see
them without being handed evidence access to do it.

200.description: Every source this service has observed.

post.summary: Stop using a source, immediately and across every in-flight run
post.description:
**Effective mid-run.** The pipeline rechecks source access immediately before each
call it makes, so a run that started an hour ago stops using this source on its very
next request. Checking only at plan time would mean a source suspended for a rights
violation kept being fetched for the length of every in-flight run.

Blocked work is **recorded as a coverage gap naming the suspension**, never silently
skipped: a run that quietly consulted one fewer source reads to a reviewer as a clean
result from a search that was never made.

One person, deliberately. Stopping a source is the safe direction, and requiring a
second approver to stop fetching from a publisher who has just complained means the
fetching continues while the second approver is found. Releasing needs four eyes.

Results already produced are **not** deleted. A later read of them shows that the
source has since been suspended (`sourceSuspendedSince` on the finding document, and
`sinceSuspendedSources` on the findings page).

post.summary: Resume using a suspended source (four eyes)
post.description: The releaser must not be the person who engaged the switch. A source is normally suspended because somebody believes we should not be fetching it, and the person who formed that belief is the wrong person to decide unilaterally that it no longer holds. Releasing also closes the breaker, whose accumulated failures describe the suspension rather than the source.

post.summary: Create a tenant
post.description:
Open signup (decision **D-053**): no invite code, and both key kinds are granted from day one.

Creates four records in **one transaction** — the tenant, its entitlement, its taxonomy version and its policy version. All four or none: a tenant missing its taxonomy is one whose first search fails with `INVALID_POLICY`, which reads as a defect in search rather than as a signup that stopped halfway.

**The tenant id is generated and cannot be requested.** There is no field for one and the schema is strict, so sending `tenantId` is refused with `UNKNOWN_FIELD` rather than ignored. A caller who could name their own id could name somebody else's.

**A live key is not available immediately.** The entitlement grants `live`, but a self-signed-up tenant must confirm its contact address first (decision **D-052**) — live searches reach real publishers under the provider's identity, against a rate budget shared across every tenant. The `liveAccess` object in the response says whether live is available and, if not, what would change that.

Signups are bounded per client address. Past that bound the answer is `429`, which is retryable: the same request succeeds once the window has passed.

**The password creates the tenant's administrator**, in the same transaction as the tenant itself (I2, decision **D-051**). It is stored as an argon2id hash and is returned by nothing. It is refused if it is too short, a known-bad value, or contains the email address or the organisation name — all three are things an attacker holding a customer list tries first.

The email address is the sign-in identity, so it must be unique: a second signup with the same address answers `409 EMAIL_ALREADY_REGISTERED`. This is the **one** route that reveals whether an address is a customer, and D-057 records why — it has to answer with a tenant id, so it cannot answer identically for both cases. Every other account route does.

201.description: The tenant, its versions, and whether it may hold a live key.

post.summary: Confirm the email address a tenant signed up with
post.description:
The token arrives by email and **is** the credential — a customer confirming an address has nothing else to present. It works once and expires.

This is the call that unlocks a live key (decision **D-052**). It sets `emailVerifiedAt` on the tenant, which is the value key issuance reads, so `liveAccessUnlocked` in the response is the same answer `POST /v1/tenant/api-keys` will give — computed by the same function, not restated.

`200`, not 201: nothing is created.

An unusable token answers `400` with one undifferentiated message, whether it is unknown, expired or already spent. A caller able to tell those apart could probe which links were issued, and the answer is the same either way: ask for a new one.

200.description: Confirmed, and whether that made a live key available.

post.summary: Send the confirmation link again
post.description:
`202`, always, with the same sentence — for an address that has an account, one that does not, and one already confirmed.

That is deliberate. An endpoint that answered differently would be a list of this service's customers, readable by anybody with a word list. The same rule governs the password-reset request; signup is the documented exception, because it has to answer with a tenant id.

202.description: Accepted. Says nothing about whether anything was sent.

post.summary: Ask for a password-reset link
post.description:
Public, because a customer who has lost their password has no credential to present.

`202`, always, with the same sentence for every address — see `/v1/signup/resend-verification` for why.

202.description: Accepted. Says nothing about whether the address has an account.

post.summary: Set a new password with an emailed token
post.description:
The token works once and expires after an hour — it is a live credential for whoever holds it, so it is deliberately short-lived.

**A reset ends every session that user holds**, and the response says how many. A reset may be an account being taken back from somebody who should not have it, and leaving the other party signed in would make the reset cosmetic. It also clears a lockout: whoever holds the mailbox has proved more than a password would.

The new password meets the same bar as a signup password, checked **before** the token is spent — so a weak choice can be corrected with the same link rather than a new one.

200.description: The password is changed and every session for that user has ended.

post.summary: Issue an API key for your own tenant
post.description:
Self-service issuance (decision **D-050**, replacing the deferral in D-007).

The `secret` in the response is shown **once** and is not recoverable: only a hash is stored, so no endpoint can return it again and no support process can recover it.

Three limits apply, and each is a rule rather than an oversight:

- a key can carry only roles **you already hold**;
- the tenant comes from your credential and can never be sent in the body;
- an `environment: "live"` key requires your tenant to be entitled to live **and** your own credential to be live. Entitlement is sold by the provider; self-service issues within what was sold.

Requires the `apikey:manage` permission, which `tenant_admin` holds.

201.description: The key, including the only copy of its secret you will ever receive.

get.description:
Every key this tenant holds, with no secret and no hash of one. `status` is derived at read time rather than stored, so a key whose expiry passed while nothing was running still reads as `EXPIRED`.

`status` names one reason a key is unusable, ordered by what you would have to do about it: `REVOKED` and `EXPIRED` mean issue a new one, `DISABLED` means enable it. A key that was disabled and has since expired therefore reads `EXPIRED`, with `disabledAt` still set to say it was also paused.

delete.description:
Immediate and irreversible. The reason is mandatory and is written to the audit trail.

A key belonging to another tenant answers **404**, not 403 — the second would confirm that it exists.

post.summary: Switch one of your keys off, reversibly
post.description:
The key stops authenticating immediately, and `POST .../enable` brings it back with the same secret and the same key id.

**This is not the one to use for a leaked secret.** Anything reversible is the wrong answer to a credential somebody else now holds — use `DELETE`, which is permanent. Disabling is for a paused integration, a rotation window, or a key you want out of service while a question is answered.

Idempotent: disabling an already-disabled key succeeds and writes no second audit entry. A **revoked** key answers `409 ALREADY_TERMINAL` — revocation cannot be undone, and accepting this call would suggest it could.

The reason is mandatory and is audited with the actor. A key belonging to another tenant answers **404**, not 403.

200.description: Disabled. The key is refused until it is enabled again.

post.summary: Turn a disabled key back on
post.description:
The same secret works again the moment this returns — nothing is re-issued and the key id does not change, so a tenant configuration that still holds it needs no edit.

Idempotent on a key that is already on. A **revoked** key answers `409 ALREADY_TERMINAL`: `revokedAt` is one-way and this route cannot touch it.

An expired key can be enabled, and will still be refused — expiry is a different reason, and the listing reports it as `EXPIRED` rather than `DISABLED`.

Error400.description: The request body or query is malformed, or carries an unknown field. Possible codes: VALIDATION_FAILED, UNKNOWN_FIELD.

Error401.description: No valid credential. The session may have expired. Possible codes: UNAUTHENTICATED, SESSION_EXPIRED, TOKEN_INVALID.

Error403.description: Authenticated, but not permitted. An entitlement denial is reported here and is never retryable (REL-02). Possible codes: FORBIDDEN, CROSS_TENANT_DENIED, ADVERSE_MEDIA_NOT_INCLUDED_IN_PLAN, SANDBOX_CANNOT_ACCESS_LIVE, BREAK_GLASS_REQUIRED.

Error404.description: Not found. Deliberately indistinguishable from an unauthorised read, so IDs cannot be enumerated. Possible codes: NOT_FOUND.

Error409.description: Conflict: a stale revision, or an idempotency key reused with a different body. Possible codes: REVISION_CONFLICT, IDEMPOTENCY_KEY_REUSED_WITH_DIFFERENT_BODY, ALREADY_TERMINAL, EMAIL_ALREADY_REGISTERED.

example.message: The record changed since it was read. Re-read it and retry.

Error413.description: The request exceeds a documented input bound. Possible codes: PAYLOAD_TOO_LARGE, INPUT_BOUND_EXCEEDED.

example.message: The request exceeds the 256 kB body limit.

Error422.description: The request is well-formed but the scope or policy it asks for is not valid. Possible codes: INVALID_SCOPE, INVALID_POLICY.

example.message: The requested scope includes a jurisdiction that is not enabled.

Error429.description: Throttled. This is not an entitlement denial and not a coverage gap. Possible codes: RATE_LIMITED.

example.message: Too many requests. Retry after the interval in the Retry-After header.

Error500.description: Unexpected failure. The body never carries internal detail (SEC-04). Possible codes: INTERNAL.

example.message: The request could not be completed.

Error501.description: A reserved endpoint that is documented but deliberately not implemented. Possible codes: NOT_IMPLEMENTED.

example.message: This endpoint is reserved and not implemented in this release.

Cursor.name: cursor
Cursor.description: Opaque continuation token from the previous page. Clients must not construct or parse one: it encodes a stable ordering key, which is what lets a page neither duplicate nor drop items while the underlying set changes.

CsrfToken.name: X-CSRF-Token
CsrfToken.description: Required for state-changing requests authenticated by the session cookie. Echoes the readable `csrf_token` cookie. Machine callers send no cookie and do not use it.

sessionCookie.name: adverse_session
sessionCookie.description: The control panel session (section 4.2). HTTP-only and secure; the browser never holds a provider token. State-changing requests must also send `X-CSRF-Token`, echoing the readable `csrf_token` cookie issued alongside it.

machineToken.description: Machine-to-machine access (section 4.2). Short-lived, audience-bound and signed with an asymmetric algorithm. Scopes are checked per route, and a `sandbox` credential can never run a live search or reach live evidence.

apiKey.name: Authorization
apiKey.description: An environment-scoped API key, sent as `Authorization: ApiKey erly_<environment>_…`. The secret is shown once at issue and stored only as a hash, so a lost key is rotated rather than recovered. Rotation invalidates the previous secret immediately, with no grace period, and both rotation and revocation are audited. A `sandbox` key can never run a live search or reach live evidence, whatever its roles say. Tenant self-service management of these keys is deferred by decision D-007; keys are provider-issued.
